title: FATAL ELECTRIC BICYCLE ACCIDENT
full_story:
On Thursday, officers with the Flora Police Department and personnel from the Clay County Ambulance Service responded to the 1100 block of Vincennes Avenue following a report of an injured female who had been involved in a traffic crash while operating an electric bicycle.

Upon arrival, emergency personnel located the rider and immediately began providing medical care.  The rider was identified as 36-year-old Stephanie R. Lewis of Flora.  Ms. Lewis was transported by Clay County Ambulance Service to Clay County Hospital for treatment of serious injuries sustained in the crash.  She later succumbed to her injuries.

The preliminary investigation indicates that Ms. Lewis was traveling on an electric bicycle on Vincennes Avenue when, for reasons that remain under investigation, she was involved in a traffic crash.

As part of the investigation, officers reviewed surveillance video from multiple cameras in the area.  Officers were also able to identify and contact individuals whose vehicles were observed traveling through the area at the time of the incident and obtained statements from those individuals.

The investigation remains active and ongoing.  Anyone who may have witnessed the incident or who has additional information is encouraged to contact the Flora Police Department at (618) 662-9111.

The Flora Police Department extends its condolences to the family and friends of Ms. Lewis during this difficult time.

title: CLAY COUNTY BOARD MEETS
full_story:
The Clay County Board met Tuesday evening at the courthouse in Louisville. Most of the meeting was routine, but near the end, members began a discussion that could dramatically impact road maintenance in Clay County.

Chairman Joe Goodman called the meeting to order. The board quickly approved the meeting agenda and past meeting minutes. Members also approved the Claims Committee Report, which shows paid claims totaled $4,118,995 with unpaid claims of $283,430.

Clay County Hospital President/CEO Bob Sellers presented the Hospital Report. He took a moment to educate the board about The Joint Commission, the leading independent, nonprofit organization that accredits and certifies hospitals across the United States. The commission conducts unannounced on-site surveys, and they just completed their visit to Clay County Hospital. Sellers said they last visited three years ago and reported 14 minor issues. This time, that number dropped to eight. The Illinois Department of Public Health also inspected CCH and reported no findings. Sellers thanked everyone involved, including the prep team of Melissa Storck, Charlotte Cooper, and Jay Walker.  Sellers also updated the board on construction of the new Clay County Health Department on the CCH campus. Concrete work continues, and the project remains on target for completion in October/November. He then asked the board to approve medical staff credentials, and members approved the list unanimously.

Brandy Young with the Clay County Health Department presented the Board of Health report in Administrator Jeff Workman’s absence. She polled various leaders at the health department for items to share with the board. Topping the list is the excitement surrounding the new health department and its collaboration with the hospital. Young highlighted concerns about the parasite Cyclospora that spreads through fresh produce. She encourages everyone to thoroughly wash these food items before consumption. She also noted the joint effort between the health department and Flora Schools on the PLAY/Prevention Initiative grant program for families with school-age children. Young encouraged everyone to attend the next S.U.R.E. Symposium on August 11 from 9 to 4 at Oil Belt Christian Service Camp, which addresses substance use issues. The health department continues monitoring for West Nile Virus. They’ve tested 630 mosquitoes with all results negative so far, while 29 Illinois counties have reported positive results. They are also collecting ticks to test for Alpha-Gal, the syndrome linked to tick bites that can cause people to become allergic to red meat. Young noted the lone star tick, which carries it, is now being found in Illinois. She closed by mentioning that Home Health and Hospice are in transition with two retirements quickly approaching, but new staff members have been hired and are in training.

Clay County Sheriff Andy Myers presented his report and briefly discussed the roof replacement project at the courthouse. They are currently seeking bids, which are due by August 11. Myers reported the sheriff’s office has hired a new deputy who is now in training. He also noted that a deputy and K-9 Chief were returning from training when they were involved in a traffic accident. Neither were injured. Recently retired K-9 Fallax has passed away.  Lt. Cory Heuerman and Fallax are credited with numerous arrests and removing large quantities of illegal drugs from our communities.  When asked about the internet outage this past weekend, the sheriff said the denial-of-service attack affected other communities in the area as well. He added that the 911 system relied on backup service as needed.

Highway Engineer Darin Koelm presented the Engineer’s Report. He said the highway department will begin oiling and chipping county roads the first week of August. Koelm noted they are scaling back this year after voters defeated the special use tax for roads in the last election. He presented a culvert petition for Beetleweed Road in Stanford Township at a cost of $20,000, to be split evenly between the county and the township. The board approved the request.

Clay County Clerk Amy Britton presented her semi-annual report, which the board approved. Members also approved the list of election judges for the November election.

In Chairman Joe Goodman’s report, he asked the board to approve the agreement between Clay County and the University of Illinois Extension and members approved his request. Goodman then raised a topic that is sure to spark wide discussion: the possibility of Clay County assuming responsibility for township road maintenance. He emphasized there is no plan to do so at this time, but he asked people to keep an open mind. The twelve townships currently handle their local roads, but finding road commissioners and sufficient tax revenue remains difficult. Goodman turned to Board Member Troy Leonard, who explained that Perry County has already taken over township road responsibilities. Leonard said their engineer is willing to speak to Clay County residents about the process. Public meetings will need to be scheduled, and the board plans to place a non-binding informational question on the November ballot asking whether voters would support the county taking over road maintenance in the twelve townships.

As the meeting drew to a close, Goodman asked the board to adopt the Clay County Animal Control Policy, which follows state requirements and members approved it.  Goodman noted the animal shelter in Louisville needs either repairs to the outside walls or a possible addition. Animal Control Officer Kevin Clark said the pens along the wall will need to be removed during the work. Goodman added that if an addition is needed it should include quarantine pens for dogs that have bitten someone.  The board voted to seek bids for the necessary renovations.

The board then went into closed session. Results were not immediately available.

title: XENIA VILLAGE BOARD
full_story:
Trustees heard comments for engineer Brandon Bridges with Charleston Engineering.  Bridges was present to provide information on the $1,075,000 road resurfacing project planned for Church and Main streets in Xenia.  Before work on the project can begin the Village trustees have opted to perform a tittle search to determine ownership of parts of the road along Main Street across the railroad tracks.

Village Superintendent Travis Lewis shared with trustees that, “everything is flowing good” following retrofitting of the villages lift station.  Mr. Lewis also discussed with trustees road work to be done along a one mile stretch of road from Church to Cottonwood Street.  Lewis told trustees he was quoted $15,000, which includes leaving and filling, and could be paid out of the MFT.  Lewis also discussed with village trustees ditch work to address flooding in the village.  The question of who is responsible for maintaining ditches in the village has been a topic of discussion among trustees for a few months.  The issue arose when trustees began discussing how to move forward in addressing the state of properties in the village.  Regarding the ditch in question Lewis said, “The responsibility of maintaining of this ditch is split between the village and the residents” he added that he would need to request permission from residents before preforming maintenance to address flooding, but he did not foresee any objections coming from those affected.

Notices have gone out to residences whose properties are in violation of ordinances.  Trustee Terri Beckham shared that she had been approached by one village resident who requests a meeting with the mayor or the board of trustees to request clarification on what exactly puts him in violation of village ordinances.  “One mans trash is another mans treasure” he told Beckman.

Trustees also discussed needed matinee to the villages community building Including: A quote to have the roof tarred for 5 years in the amount of $136,000, Needed repairs to the gym and cafeteria floors, A section of the roof in the chaffier kitchen.  Trustees also briefly discussed constructing a new city hall but no action was taken.

Trustees passed a motion to put a new heating and cooling unit and new curtains in the meeting room, village secretary’s office before adjourning.

title: CLAY COUNTY FAIR SCHEDULE
full_story:
The Clay County Fair will start Friday, July 24th at 4 pm with the 33 annual 4H BBQ at the REA building.  Menu is a Salt & Strings pork chop, green beans, cheesy potatoes, homemade desert and drink for $12, or $5 for a hot dog meal.  You can pre-purchase tickets from Clay County 4-H members, or you can stop by the extension office at 210 S Church St., Louisville, or they can be purchased at the door.

Gates will then open at 5:30 for the Crain Scates Bucking Bulls Rodeo hosted by the Clay County Farm Bureau Young Leaders.  Cost to enter the rodeo is $15, those 5 and under get in for free, pre show tickets are available from Young Leaders and are $12.  Mutton busting will be available for $10 with only 30 spots available for children under 80 lbs.  Carnival rides will also open on Friday night.

Saturday morning July 25th starts at 8 am with the poultry and rabbit check in.  The poultry show is at 9 am followed by the 4H and JR Rabbit Show.  All livestock should be on the fairgrounds by 3 pm.  There will also be a mandatory meeting for all livestock exhibitors and vet papers check at 3 pm.  After the meeting livestock weigh in will begin, and the night ends at 7 pm with the open sheep show.

Sunday, July 26th will have the JR Sheep show at 11 am and JR Goat show at Noon.  Registration for the kids pedal tractor pull at 1 pm next to the Merchants building, and the kids pull is at 2 pm, hosted by the Clay County Farm Bureau Young Leaders.  The 4H Horse show and JR Horse show is at 2 pm.  The Clay County 4H Federation will have yard games from 5 to 7 pm.  The Clay County Ministerial Alliance program is from 5:30 to 7 pm and there will be a greased pig contest at 7 pm sponsored by UPI Fairfield.

On Monday, July 27th the fair will kick into high gear with the 4H Beef Show at 8 am followed by the JR Beef Show, AITC Activities will be in the Farm Bureau building from 2 to 4 pm.  Then at 5 pm it’s the Mini Livestock Show for those 4 to 8 years of age hosted by the Clay County Farm Bureau Young Leaders.  The night ends with the Little Miss Pageant at 7:30 pm admission is $10 for adults and $5 for kids 3 – 10.  There are 19 young ladies vying for the title held by Izzabella Brinkley.

Tuesday will be Nutrien Ag Solutions Day at the fair with giveaways and activities throughout the day.  At 8 am is the 4H Swine show and Open Beef Show, followed by the Sheep Show at 1 pm and the 4H Goat Show at 2:30 pm.  Then at 5 pm will be the Master Showmanship Contest, sponsored by the Clay County Farm Bureau Young Leaders.  On the stage at 7:30 pm will be the Junior Miss Clay County Fair Pageant and Queen pie auction.  Admission to the Junior Miss pageant is $10 for adults and $5 for kids 3 – 10.  There are 10 contestants, Halle Patridge is the current JR Miss.

Wednesday will start at 8 am with the JR Swine Show followed by the Open Goat Show.  DaS zle Dance and Tumble will perform at 5 pm, admission is free, and the 4H Livestock Auction will begin at 6:30pm.

Thursday opens at 8 am with the Open Dairy Show, then at 5 pm Joni’s Power & Grace Tumbling will be in the REA building, admission is free.  The Lickity Split and Legally Sheila concert will be on the stage 7 pm.

The Fair will culminate with the Clay County Fair Queen Pageant Friday night, July 31st at 7 pm, with admission $10 for adults and $5 for kids 3 – 10.  There are 13 young ladies vying for the title.  The current Queen is Olivia Haun.

Clay County 4H Youth Development Educator, Megan Pierson will be talking about the fair today on the ReVue.

title: CLAY COUNTY SHERIFF’S ACTIVITY REPORT
full_story:
Clay County Sheriff Andy Myers presented his monthly activity report during Tuesday’s Clay County Board meeting.  In the Report for June, the Sheriff’s Office issued a total of 23 Traffic Citations, made 39 Criminal Arrests and served 23 various Civil Papers.  A total of 20,881 miles were driven by Sheriff’s personnel during the month.

40 persons were processed through the Clay County Jail during June.  There were 9 inmates in jail at the beginning of the month and 10 in jail at the end of the month.  The average daily jail population was 10.

Also, the Clay County Sheriff’s Office received a total of $5,201 during the month.  This includes:

The Sheriff’s Office handled approximately 532 complaints, 97 of which originated in Louisville and 79 in Clay City.  The Sheriff’s Office conducted 33 Criminal Investigations and 10 Accident Investigations during June.

title: CLAY CITY VILLAGE BOARD SPECIAL MEETING
full_story:
The Clay City Village Board called a special meeting Monday afternoon at 4:00 to wrap up some unfinished business from last week’s regular meeting.

Mayor Mike Delonshaw called the meeting to order, and trustees quickly got to work. The main reason for the special session was to finalize contract changes for the village’s trash vendor, DBS Disposal. Damon Simmons told trustees last week that he is selling the business to Steve Stortzum of Louisville. Simmons asked the board to approve a revised contract that removes his name and adds Stortzum. Services will stay exactly the same, and Stortzum pledged he will be available through the business phone number. Trustees made a motion to approve the updated contract language, and they passed it unanimously.

Trustees also learned last week that the village is now down one service vehicle, and the remaining one is nearing the end of its useful life. Mayor Delonshaw presented a proposal from Eagleson Automotive in Olney. The Board is now considering whether to purchase one replacement vehicle or add a second vehicle. The mayor asked trustees to compare options from other local dealers, including regular cab and crew cab models. The board tabled the issue until a future meeting so members can make better comparisons.

The meeting moved along quickly until trustees took up the Appropriations Ordinance. Village Attorney Barry Bright explained that the figures in the ordinance are estimates of what the village may need to spend in the coming year. He reminded the board that the document serves as a wish list rather than an actual budget or automatic approval to spend money. Trustees must still vote on any specific expenditure at a later date.  Trustee Sue Lindeman said she understands spending must rise over time, but she questioned why this year’s ordinance runs one million dollars higher than last year’s. Trustees Jim Duff and Larry Phillips also pushed back, saying the village needs to rein in spending. After some back-and-forth discussion, Trustee Beth Prosser, attending remotely, helped clarify the process. Phillips and Duff agreed with her explanation. Trustee Travis Strasbaugh then made a motion to approve the ordinance. Prosser seconded it, and the board passed the measure four-to-one, with Lindeman voting no.

Next, trustees discussed the tax levy for the new year. Attorney Bright explained the village can raise the levy by up to 4.9 percent without triggering extra requirements. If they raise it by 5 percent or more, they must advertise the hearing in the newspaper at a cost of over $600 and hold a truth-in-taxation hearing so taxpayers can speak their mind. Since action isn’t required until later this year, the board decided to table the issue until September.

Another lengthy discussion focused on action the board took last week to help Ali Hilderbrand move her business, Ali’s Beauty Barn, to Clay City behind Casey’s. Attorney Bright said the previous action was improper. Trustees had agreed to sell her a lot for just ten dollars and cover utility installation. Bright noted the village last sold a lot at that price for residential use, not commercial. The board voted to rescind last week’s decision and looked for other ways to help Hilderbrand.  After several suggestions fell through due to their location or the high cost of installing water and sewer lines, someone proposed leasing the original property to her for one year while the village covers the utility hookups. Hilderbrand agreed, with the understanding she can keep looking for a permanent site and cancel the lease with 30 days’ notice. She will pay the village fifty dollars per month plus her own water, sewer, and electric costs. Trustees approved the agreement. The board called another special meeting for Monday, July 20 at 4:00 p.m., if Attorney Bright is available, to keep the project moving.

The mayor also mentioned that another person is interested in placing a modular home in Sunset Acres, but the board needs more information before making a decision.

Finally, trustees turned to the ongoing issue of nuisance properties. Attorney Bright said the Nuisance Committee should meet and create a list of targeted properties. He gave them a document outlining seven required steps. Bright agreed to contact the property owner and give them ten days to clean up. If they don’t comply, the village can take them to court, where owners could face up to $850 in fines and court costs. The board agreed to move forward with that approach, starting with the property at 225 South 4th Street SW. With all business complete, the meeting adjourned.
